findings.explanation: Different agents claim the same implementation tasks 5–7 [M3][M4], then each reports completing all three with identical output paths [M6][M7]. A third agent claims and later completes T7 as well [M5][M11]. These are materially equivalent execution claims with no stated verification, synthesis, or handoff purpose; the finding does not depend on treating deliberate checks as duplication.

Ownership is visibly inconsistent: the initial split assigns c3=T4 and c4=T5–7 [M2], c3 instead claims T5–7 and assigns c4=T4 [M3], c4 also claims T5–7 [M4], and c2 claims T7 conditionally [M5]. Multiple agents subsequently report the same outputs [M6][M7][M11], without a visible reconciliation of that overlap. c3's later T4 claim resolves its circuit ownership [M8], not the earlier overlapping execution.

The conflicting early splits [M2][M3][M4][M5] and repeated completion reports [M6][M7][M11] support ownership overlap, but do not establish that a later decision ignored relevant information despite a clear opportunity to use it. The candidates expose neither the execution start times nor a later synthesis requiring those results. c3 does take T4 [M8]. Missing acknowledgement alone is insufficient to prove information was not integrated.
